one_liner: C++ WebAssembly runtime whose LLVM AOT mode ties Wasmtime and beats V8 and wazero on libsodium; its interpreter is slow.
what_it_does: Embeddable WebAssembly runtime (libwasmedge shared or static library plus the wasmedge CLI) with WASI, Wasm 3.0 proposals, a component-model implementation in progress and plug-ins for WASI-NN (llama.cpp, whisper), sockets, crypto and more. Hosts embed it through its own C API (wasmedge.h), the standard wasm.h C API added in 0.18.0, or Go/Rust SDKs; it is not API-compatible with Wasmtime or Wasmer. Run modes are interpreter (the default), AOT, JIT and, since 0.18.0, lazy JIT, picked with --run-mode or the RunMode configuration.
how_it_is_fast: Speed comes from ahead-of-time compilation: `wasmedge compile` (formerly wasmedgec) lowers Wasm to LLVM IR, optimises it at O2 by default (O0-O3, s, z selectable) and emits a native shared library or a 'universal Wasm' file carrying the native code in a custom section, tuned for the host CPU name and features unless --generic-binary is given. 0.18.0 also inlines memory.size, table.size/get/set and the call_indirect dispatch into compiled code and maps SIMD min/max/abs to LLVM intrinsics. The interpreter is a plain switch dispatch over the loaded instruction list with an operand-stack manager (lib/executor/engine/engine.cpp), with no register-IR rewrite, which is why it trails the faster interpreters.
when_to_use: Long-running server or edge workloads where you can AOT-compile modules ahead of deployment and want near-Wasmtime or better throughput: 64-bit-multiply-heavy crypto (ed25519, curve25519 box/sign/scalarmult) ran in 0.55-0.60x Wasmtime's time in the 2022-12 libsodium run.
Workloads that should beat V8/Node.js or wazero on compute: geomean 0.86x Node's time and 0.21x wazero's over 61 libsodium tests.
When you need the WasmEdge ecosystem: LlamaEdge/WASI-NN inference plug-ins, crun and runwasi Kubernetes integration, WasmEdge socket and database extensions.
C or C++ hosts that want a C API (including wasm.h since 0.18.0) and a CMake build, on Linux x86-64/aarch64, macOS, Windows, Android or OpenHarmony.
when_not_to_use: If you want the fastest AOT engine: in the same 2022-12 libsodium data WAMR's LLVM AOT (iwasm) and wasm2c were about 1.46x and 1.42x faster and Wasmer LLVM 1.16x faster; the 2026 rerun (search snippet only) still puts WAMR AOT at 1.57-1.59x native against WasmEdge's 1.74x.

Interpreter-only deployments (iOS, W^X, no LLVM): the interpreter was 8.42x (M4 Max E-cores) and 9.28x (A12) the fastest of seven interpreters in the 2026-09-22 rebeckerspecialties comparison, against 1.01-1.04x for wasm3 and 1.38-1.63x for WAMR fast-interp; in the wasmi-benchmarks execute geomean it was x145.74 of the fastest on EPYC 7763 (x142.45 M4 Pro, x110.01 Xeon 8573C) against x12.40 for Wasmi v2; issue #2748 timed it at 91.5 s against 15.2 s for Wasmi and 17.7 s for WAMR on one module.
Small-call, SHA-2/HMAC-heavy guest code: WasmEdge took 2.2-3.4x Wasmtime's time on libsodium hash, hash3, auth, auth2, auth6 and kdf in 2022-12, while winning on curve arithmetic.
Multi-threaded hosts sharing one VM: the README says 'Currently, WasmEdge is not yet thread-safe'.

Wasm GC guests that allocate continuously: the interpreter never collected GC structs during an instance's lifetime in the 2026-09-22 comparison (gc_trees peaked at 295 MB and still held 145 MB after the case).

integration.form: shared lib (libwasmedge) or static lib, CMake build; prebuilt CLI and libraries via installer
integration.dependencies: LLVM and LLD for AOT/JIT (WASMEDGE_USE_LLVM, on by default; off gives an interpreter-only build); spdlog, fmt, simdjson and blake3 (system copies or pinned FetchContent copies); Threads; std::filesystem; zstd/zlib when linking LLVM statically; plug-ins pull their own (OpenSSL, llama.cpp, OpenCV, ...)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 compiler, CMake 3.18; LLVM version handling covers roughly LLVM 13 through 23 in the build scripts (exact minimum not documented)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and aarch64, macOS x86-64 and Apple silicon, Windows 10, Android, seL4, OpenWrt, OpenHarmony, Raspberry Pi, s390x; RISC-V marked work in progress
integration.thread_safety: README: 'Currently, WasmEdge is not yet thread-safe'; 0.18.0 removed getter locks from the hot path and fixed data races in store teardown, but no thread-safety guarantee is documented.

gotchas: Harness trap: since 0.17.0 the default run mode is the interpreter and an AOT-compiled universal Wasm file runs interpreted (its native section ignored) unless --run-mode=aot is passed; since 0.18.0 (PR #5292) a native .so input is rejected outright without it. A script in the style of libsodium's wasi-test-wrapper.sh (`wasmedgec x.wasm x.so && wasmedge x.so`) therefore measures the interpreter on 0.17.x and fails on 0.18.0; the 2026 rerun had to force --run-mode=aot.

The 2022-12 numbers come from libsodium's own harness: the wrapper runs `wasm-opt -O4` on every module, AOT-compiles with wasmedgec and runs the .so, and cmptest.h times ITERATIONS calls of the test body inside the guest with clock_gettime and printf compiled out. Startup and AOT compile time are therefore excluded, so WasmEdge's 2-3x losses on the short tests are not process startup as the verifier assumed; the cause is unidentified. A candidate: WasmEdge AOT indirect calls were about 10x slower than WAMR's (issue #2444: 1M function-pointer calls 26.8 ms vs 2.77 ms; closed by PR #5088, and 0.18.0 inlined call_indirect dispatch in #4613), and libsodium routes poly1305 and randombytes through function-pointer tables. The WasmEdge version, compiler and flags of the 2022-12 run are not recorded.

AOT artifacts are host-specific native code loaded with dlopen: they target the build machine's CPU features unless --generic-binary is used, the AOT binary format was bumped to version 3 in 0.18.0 (older artifacts must be recompiled), and before PR #5292 a .so's initialisers ran at load time even in interpreter mode, so only load AOT files you built yourself.

Security: CVE-2025-69261 (GHSA-89fm-8mr7-gg4m, integer wrap in MemoryInstance::getSpan's size check) was fixed in 0.15.1, and 0.18.0 lists many hardening fixes (WASI symlink escape outside the preopen, OOB write via stale try_table handlers, memory64 bounds checks in AOT); only 0.17.1 and 0.16.4 are listed as supported in SECURITY.md.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick WasmEdge over WAMR or wasm2c when you need its WASI-NN/LlamaEdge plug-ins, Kubernetes integrations or full Wasm 3.0 support in AOT, and can accept AOT code about 1.4x slower than WAMR AOT or wasm2c on libsodium; for interpreter-only targets pick wasm3, WAMR fast-interp or Wasmi instead, since WasmEdge's interpreter was 5-12x slower than theirs (8.42 vs 1.01-1.63 on M4 Max E-cores; x145.74 vs x12.40-17.07 on EPYC 7763 in wasmi-benchmarks).
verified_claims_summary: In Frank Denis's 2022-12 libsodium WebAssembly run (jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks CSVs; per the blocked 2023 post a Zen 2 Scaleway instance with tests pinned to one core), WasmEdge AOT took 0.97x Wasmtime's time, 1.00x Wasmer Cranelift's, 0.86x Node/V8's and 0.21x wazero's, but 1.16x Wasmer LLVM's, 1.46x WAMR AOT's and 1.42x wasm2c's (geomean over the 61 tests with a native result; I recomputed these from the CSVs), and 3.35x native; including the 8 short tests without a native result it is 1.07x slower than Wasmtime. The README's 'fastest Wasm VM' claim rests on the authors' own 2021 IEEE Software paper, which is not reachable here, and is not supported by this independent data.
status_note: Very active CNCF sandbox project (0.18.0 released 2026-10-05, Apache-2.0, 10.8k stars) usable as a library today, but it is a large LLVM-dependent C++ code base and its benchmark speed depends on using AOT mode explicitly.
